Medical professionalism is predicated on the Hippocratic Oath. Most physicians adhere to an
updated version written by Louis Lasagna in 1964.
The best-known core principle in medical ethics is Primum non nocere, or “First, do no harm.”
This aphorism, which probably was written in the 17th century by Thomas Sydenham, an
English physician, does not appear in the Hippocratic Oath. It is intended to give a physician
pause before automatically recommending surgical management (which may result in
complications), prescribing a medicine (which may have adverse effects), or ordering a test
(which may have false-positive results, provoking anxiety or resulting in inappropriate
management).
A fundamental tenet of professionalism is that a patient’s interests should always be foremost.
Maintaining this principle can be a challenge in a fee-for-service medical environment, in which
volume- and price-related incentives may affect decision making.
Modern professional principles include an emphasis on privacy (which, in the United States, is
codified in the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996) and patient
empowerment (informed consent).
Modern professionalism assumes good medical record keeping and accurate billing.

Professionalism and Code of Ethics
The principles of autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice form the
foundations of the principles ethics. This ethical methodology is largely considered one
of the most appropriate paradigms for approaching medical decision making1 (Resource
1).
Informed Consent
Informed consent is predicated on respect for persons and their right to make autonomous
decisions.
Informed consent depends on providing adequate information so the patient can decide, for
example, which therapeutic option to follow or whether to enroll in a research study.
Alternative treatment options should be presented.
The risks and advantages of each option should be described.

The language should be clear and free of jargon.
Most of the clinical consent process is oral. The written document should highlight the most
important points made during the oral discussion.
The physician obtaining consent should make a good-faith effort to evaluate whether the
patient understands the information that has been provided.
Patients have the right to decide their own course of treatment, even if their decisions are bad
from the physician’s point of view.
Patients should be aware that their decision to proceed with treatment is voluntary.
In clinical care, deciding whether written consent or oral consent is required usually is based
on risk. For most invasive procedures, written consent is expected. For minor procedures (eg,
phlebotomy), consent usually is tacit (understood) or oral. Written informed consent
underscores that a serious decision is being made.
True informed consent requires three key elements: the provision of adequate information,
comprehension of the information by the person being asked to consent, and voluntariness.
“Respect for a patient’s autonomy is considered a fundamental ethical principle. Autonomy
denotes the capacity of a rational individual to make an informed, uncoerced decision. This
belief is central to the premise of the concept of informed consent. The principle of
confidentiality is also essential in patient autonomy. A [patient] must give informed consent for
confidential information to be divulged to [other entities].”1
Industry Relationships
Medical research relationships with industry are not intrinsically bad.
Physician­–industry relationships fall into several categories: employment, scientific
collaborations, clinical, and marketing.
Industry may sponsor research by a physician or group of physicians.
To minimize the potential for bias, physician researchers working with industry and charged
with writing study-related manuscripts should request access to the raw research data;
however, this is not the industry research norm.
Close relationships with industry may produce bias, particularly if personal compensation
depends on a particular outcome. For example, if a physician invents and then licenses a
product, resulting in a royalty stream, positive results from a study of that product may
increase the inventor’s personal income. This type of relationship can reduce the credibility
of the research if the inventor takes a key role. Biased research results also may be harmful
to future patients.

In academic medical centers, research contracts generally are agreements between the
institution and the company, whereas for physicians in private practice, the contract usually
is between the practice and the sponsor or contract research organization. Contracts with
academic medical centers are more complicated because universities, as nonprofit entities,
must work in the public benefit. In research, that usually means assurance that the work will
be published. Also, many academic medical centers include language in their contracts that
allows them to retain the rights to new intellectual property. Because private practices rarely
pay attention to either of these issues, those practices have contractual advantages from the
point of view of many sponsors.
For National Institutes of Health grants, the US Public Health Service requires reporting of all
major financial interests that may directly and substantially affect the design, conduct, or
reporting of research. This responsibility falls on the institution that receives the grant,
usually an academic institution or nonprofit organization. To help the institution identify
which financial interests to report, investigators are required to fully disclose their financial
relationships, after which the conflict-of-interest program is expected to manage any
conflicts.
Typical management strategies include a requirement for disclosure of external financial
relationships.
Institutional review boards (IRBs) often require informed-consent documents to provide
information about external financial interests.
The National Institutes of Health expects the institution to describe how its management
approach will mitigate bias related to conflicts of interest in the research. The institution is
required to file a formal report with the US Public Health Service.

Industry Relationships
As of 2013, the Physician Payments Sunshine Act (part of the Affordable Care Act of
2010) publicly documents physician–industry relationships, requiring pharmaceutical
companies, device manufacturers, and medical service providers to report all payments
of $10 or more made to physicians and academic medical centers. These reports are
summarized in a publicly accessible, searchable website so all physician–industry
financial arrangements become public knowledge.

Clinical Medical Research
IRBs evaluate research protocols for scientific validity, ethical design, and proposed conduct.
Federally sponsored research is regulated by the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). Regulation
45 CFR §46, known as the Common Rule, also is applied to most other human investigations in
in the United States.
The FDA has its own set of rules set down in regulation 21 CFR §50 and §56, which are similar
to the Common Rule but add requirements related to FDA jurisdiction.
The Common Rule is based largely on the Belmont Report, a 1979 document written by the
National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral
Research, or just the National Commission.
The National Commission was created in response to several research scandals, including
the Tuskegee syphilis study, in which investigators appeared to prioritize scientific objectives
over the health and well-being of the individuals who took part in the research. In some
cases, the study participants were neither aware of nor informed that they were involved in
research.
The Belmont Report codifies three basic principles for the ethical conduct of clinical research.
Respect for persons—Individuals have autonomous rights to participate in research (or
not), and their decisions should be made based on an informed consent process.
Beneficence—Research should benefit the participants or people like them.
Justice—The selection of research subjects should be fair.
Before human subjects enroll in a research study in the United States, the research proposal
must be submitted to an IRB. Internationally, most institutions and countries have ethics
review boards that serve the same function as IRBs.
“Events of the late nineteenth century and surrounding World War II spawned concerns about
how research was conducted, which led to the foundations of modern research ethics. In the
late nineteenth century, yellow fever was a raging epidemic in Cuba. Giuseppe Sanarelli, an
Italian bacteriologist, injected 5 people with an organism that he thought caused yellow fever,
resulting in severe harm and wide criticism. After this incident, the US Surgeon General
commissioned Walter Reed to identify the cause of yellow fever. Reed developed ethical
guidelines for this research, which were implemented by the US Army’s Yellow Fever Board.
This Board is considered the predecessor of today’s Research Ethics Committee (REC).
“Later, the Nuremberg Code of 1947 was drafted in connection with the Nuremberg trials after
World War II. The main principles of the Code were that informed consent is necessary, that
research should yield results that are for the good of society, and that risks to research

Ethical Issues for the Sports Medicine Team Physician
“Many ethical issues are unique to sports medicine because of the unusual clinical
environment of caring for athletes within the context of a team whose primary goal is to win.
The tension that can arise when trying to balance medical means with nonmedical ends can be
challenging.”4
The traditional doctor–patient relationship is replaced with a doctor–patient–team triad1
Conflict of Interest
Physicians engaged in sports medicine, particularly the care of professional athletes, often are
caught in a conflict-of-interest situation because their employer is the team and their patients
are athletes who play for the team.
Some decisions pit a player’s best interests against those of the team. A decision to play
despite the risk of long-term injury should be made by a fully informed player who has
received independent advice. Players should be allowed to seek second opinions from
independent physicians.
“Confidentiality, a fundamental to the practice of medicine, is altered by the team physician’s
dual responsibilities to the player-patient and the team. Documents constructed by the team
generally specify the parameters by which health information may be handled. Oftentimes,
these ground rules are not truly understood by the player or the clinician. Even in the best of
circumstances, situations will arise that will challenge the clinician’s judgment as to handling of
confidential health information. The team doctor should make a strong effort to understand
the rules of handling personal health information, and seek to discuss these issues with both
the player-patients and team administration in hopes of preempting or minimizing conflicts.
Clinical decision making in sports medicine may manifest conflicts of competing interests–

short term pursuits of competition and success versus long term health. Team physicians must
assist the player-patient in determining their priorities, and be aware of other influences that
may negatively affect the pursuit of the primary interest(s).”5 (Resource 3)
Confidentiality
Rules surrounding privacy may not be clear in a team setting.
The team physician is part of the team.
Good medical care requires the confidence of the patient/player, including confidence in the
privacy of information.
The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act generally does not cover physicians
employed by a team in their communication with the team. Therefore, confidentiality
decisions mainly reflect professional ethics and personal discretion, rather than legal
principles.
“Ethics refers to idealized codes of behavior and consequently sports medicine ethics cannot
be seen as unique or subject to lesser standards. However, it is true that the social context in
which sports medicine ethics are operationalized has distinct characteristics and manifestly
structures the behavior of those charged with the duty to act ethically. Studies of the practice
of maintaining patient confidentiality in sports medicine show, for example, that the distinct
physical environment, practice, and policy context of sports medicine, and the conflicts of
interest that stem from multiple obligations, shape how patient confidentiality is maintained.
Breaches in confidentiality are common and there is considerable variation within and
between professional groups regarding the maintenance of patient confidentiality. However,
there are a variety of actions that could be taken to bolster ethical practice in sport in relation
to patient confidentiality and this implementation is vital to uphold the status and influence of
sports medicine.”6 (Resource 4)
Standard of Care in the Professional Athlete
Controversy exists regarding whether a separate legal standard of care should apply to the
treatment of professional athletes. Poma et al7 proposed a single standard of care model to
minimize conflicts for team physicians:
“Team owners, coaches, and professional players themselves may have a variety of interests
that supersede considerations for the player’s health, those interests should play no role in the
physician–patient relationship. The team physician’s obligation is to operate within the
